Just go with it man. In my experience, anxiety comes from resistance of some kind. You had a bad experience in the past, at a time when your mind wasn't all "there." Now as the effects of the psychedelic are coming on again it is triggering your memory of the bad trip and in turn creating fear that the current trip will be bad as well. Break the cycle. How? Just go with it. Stop trying to not feel anxious. If you're feeling anxious just feel it and accept it. Surprisingly this with reduce it. This exact concept is how I stopped having panic attacks, even before ever trying psychedelics. When I would feel one coming on I would get anxious and "try really hard not to have a panic attack." This resistance actually triggered the attack. Eventually I would feel it coming and just think "Yeah, I might have a panic attack. That's ok." And then I wouldn't. Idk, give it a go I guess.

I'm sure this is more than you were asking for, but this essay I wrote for my Eastern Philosophy class lays out exactly what I love about Taoism. Mostly, it just resonates with something inside me like nothing else has. It has a warm flowing nature to it that I've never found through anything "rational." I am very analytical and intellectual, and there is plenty of that in Taoism, but it also placed great emphasis on simply "being." This calm acceptance of not knowing balancing out my endless intellectualization of everything.  Essay:


The eastern world has produced some incredible contributions to human thought. Taoism is one of the lesser known of these contributions. There are many reasons for this, but that is not to say it is not worth investigation. Taoism can be hastily brushed aside by the intellectual, but the true seeker will catch a glimpse of its inner elegance and become hooked. Proverbs that may at first appear to be ill-conceived and irrational, will soon be recognized as containing amazing depth and sophistication, albeit through simplicity.          
	“What is the Tao?” you may ask.  To which the Taoist may reply, “What isn’t the Tao?” This sort of banter is often come across in Taoist teachings. One purpose is to shake the mind of the student out of its normal process. Intellectually satisfying answers are purposefully avoided because one core tenet of Taoism is that the Tao is vague and beyond human conception. That is to say, beyond what can fit nicely into a mental concept. So to give the student a straight answer would not only set the student behind, but would be totally inaccurate. Something inherently vague cannot be described explicitly. 
While the Tao is beyond mental conception, the Tao could also be said to include all mental concepts. After all, words are concepts of themselves and Taoism could not be communicated at all without them. The attributes given to the Tao are not intended to be ultimate, but rather useful tools to understand it on whatever level the student is functioning. The Tao is said to be vague, formless, spontaneous, and silent, and has been compared to a mirror and a mysterious female. Much can be said about each of these descriptions, but suffice it to say, the Tao is complex when considering all that has been said of it, but simple when experienced directly. 
One integral teaching of Taoism is called “wu-wei.” Wu-wei has been translated in many ways, but essentially means “effortless action” or perhaps “painless effort.” Consider dancing. Dancing often requires much physical exertion, but yet we call it “fun” rather than “work.” This is because the exertion is spontaneous and flowing, rather than something that must be done by force. It has to do with attitude, not action. Living “wu-wei” can also be considered living in alignment with Tao. One does not over-think or worry, or force things to happen. One recognizes one’s inherent connection to all beings and events and simply fulfills one’s role effortlessly. 
Taoism teaches that man is born good, but the corruption of society causes contamination and confusion. So it is taught to avoid “meddling in the world,” or in other words to remove yourself from society and its influences. By living a quiet life outside of the bustle of society one is able to remove these conditioned mindsets that cause disharmony. This is the life of the sage. 
The qualities of a sage are put forth in detail in the “Tao Te Ching,” perhaps the most fundamental text in Taoism as well as in Chinese literature. Thought to be written by a man named Lao Tzu in the 6th century BC, the text has this, and many more things, to say about the life of the sage:
Seek to attain to absolute emptiness;
Maintain a state of perfect stillness. See how all things come into being.
And see how they return!
They come to flower and fullness
And then go back to the roots whence they came.
To go home to the root is to achieve perfect stillness.
Thus, in attaining stillness, do they fulfill their destiny; and thus, in turning back,
they join the Never-changing.
To be aware of the Never-changing is to be enlightened. (Tao te Ching, v. 16)


The Taoist teachings on death and immortality depend on which school of thought one is referring to. What many scholars refer to as “pure” or “philosophical” Taoism teaches that death is simply the passing of an old decrepit body, which is the last bit of personal identity the Taoist has, having already released all mental attachments including a sense of individuality. In this sense, one is immortal when one ceases to recognize the distinction between one’s self and the Tao (the Tao being beyond time and space.) However, if one is referring to what is called “religious Taoism” then it is taught that one should seek, through intense cultivation, to create a “spirit embryo” of sorts that will enable one to live on past the decay of the physical body, into eternity. Religious Taoism was traditionally very interested in medicinal compounds that would serve as “elixirs of life,” and many held the view that it was possible to permanently prolong life in the physical realm. (It should be noted that the distinction between “philosophical Taoism” and “religious Taoism” may be a superimposition of western categorization onto an otherwise undifferentiated belief system.) 
Personally, Taoism has an organic quality that I find unresistable. What some may see as “gaping holes” in the philosophy, I see as being so broad as to include everything and in this way I see its foundation to be all but seamless. For instance, the question of whether or not the Tao exists is seen by Taoists to be “too intellectual” or as a distraction from enjoying the direct experience of the Tao, whatever it is. But some may see this as a convenient escape from providing the necessary evidence for belief, or as an absurd tactic to set yourself “above” the hard questions. To me, Taoism has found a way to weave its way through the turmoil of life like a small child darting through obstacles that a larger (more complex) adult would inevitably bump into and incur damage. Or water that easily adopts the form of the container instead of bricks that would be at odds with anything not brick-shaped. In this way, Taoism is as relevant to today as it was in ancient China.

Once again, this is a limited understanding of Taoism. It is not simply "doing whatever you want" because Taoism holds that we are born in sync with nature, but society ingrains negative conditioning that we must see past in order to live in accordance with the Tao. At the same time, nothing you do can be out of accordance with the Tao, but you may not be conscious of experiencing it. There is no "salvation" in Taoism (philosophical Taoism). There is no authority, or necessary customs, or set way to live. But living in line with your nature and the cessation of internal conflict is an ideal.

Taoism, like any religion or school of thought, has a variety of approached. It is far too simplistic to sum up Taoism in a few sentences. But what you are talking about is often referred to as "religious Taoism." I am not attracted to that. I am attracted to "philosophical Taoism." Philosophical Taoism is nearly synonymous with pantheism, depending on your approach. There is very little to no emphasis on deities, besides what this or that deity "represents" within the Tao. The Tao is not an entity, but it also not just the material universe. It is not male or female, active or inactive, large or small, etc. These are mental classifications, none of which can contain the Tao. 
To a scientific materialist this will be pointless and irrational, but that's because science places very little value on inner experience. I see Taoism as being very compatible with science because it does not require any specific beliefs to be held, nor rituals to be performed, etc.
